extracted.intended_audience: law scholars, patent practitioners, USPTO examiners, and policymakers interested in patent claim construction and prosecution policy
extracted.subtask_description: Scholarly analysis and policy recommendations about how patent claims should be interpreted during prosecution and litigation (BRC vs PHOSITA) and procedural changes to improve public notice. Focuses on incentives, examiner practice, and doctrinal rules (e.g., obviousness, written description) affecting claim clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public notice as primary function of patent claims
rubrics_metrics.description: A primary function of a patent is to provide public notice about the claimed invention; patents must 'apprise the public of what is still open to them' and should not contain ambiguous language or vague descriptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unclear claims harm the public by failing to mark what is in the public domain, encourage gaming, increase uncertainty, retard competition, and discourage use of unprotected ideas. The public-notice goal should guide interpretive rules and prosecution practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broadest Reasonable Construction (BRC) rule during prosecution
rubrics_metrics.description: During patent prosecution the USPTO examiner determines claim meaning by giving the proposed claims their 'broadest reasonable construction in light of the specification.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The BRC is used to determine applicable prior art and to guide the examiner's search and rejections. It was intended to (1) force iterative clarifying amendments, (2) incentivize precise initial drafting, and (3) set an outer boundary to reduce risk of unexpected broader interpretations in litigation. In practice, BRC can fail to produce these benefits and can impose costs without corresponding benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: PHOSITA rule for litigation claim construction
rubrics_metrics.description: In litigation, courts construe claim terms according to their 'ordinary and customary' meaning to a person having ordinary skill in the art (PHOSITA) at the relevant time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ordinary meaning is informed primarily by the patent's intrinsic record (specification, claims, prosecution history). Specification definitions control if present (inventor-as-lexicographer). Extrinsic evidence (dictionaries, expert testimony) may be used if ambiguity remains, but intrinsic evidence takes precedence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three methods of enhancing public notice
rubrics_metrics.description: A theoretical framework identifying three prosecution processes that could produce claim clarity: (1) iterative improvements (amendments and records), (2) ex ante incentives for precise claiming, and (3) definition of the outer limits of claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretive rules and examiner practices should be evaluated by how well they foster these three methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Iterative improvements (use prosecution to create public record)
rubrics_metrics.description: The idea that broad constructions during prosecution will make vague claims more likely to be rejected, forcing applicants to amend claims and thereby create a clarifying public record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The prosecution process is interactive: examiner rejections push applicants to narrow or clarify claims, developing written record and notice. However, this depends on active examiner enforcement and applicant responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ex ante incentives for more precise claiming (penalty-default effect)
rubrics_metrics.description: The threat of a broad construction and rejection during prosecution should incentivize applicants ex ante to draft clearer initial claims to avoid costly amendments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This functions like a penalty default—if applicants know vague claims will be broadly construed and likely rejected, they will draft more precisely. The effectiveness depends on applicants' expectations of examiner behavior and costs of prosecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of the outer limits of claims (prevent ensnarement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpretive approaches should set an outer boundary on claim meaning during prosecution to minimize the risk that potential infringers will be unfairly ensnared by broader litigation constructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: BRC was supposed to create such outer limits, but courts often interpret issued claims more broadly than the USPTO, undermining that goal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abandon BRC in prosecution; apply PHOSITA rule during prosecution
rubrics_metrics.description: Policy recommendation that pending patent applications should be construed using the same PHOSITA rule used in litigation rather than BRC.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using the PHOSITA rule in prosecution would increase consistency between prosecution and litigation, reduce harms caused by conflicting rules, and impose minimal costs since examiners could read claims in context; other procedural changes can fill any notice void created by abandoning BRC.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiners should require disclaimers and definitions (but not claim charts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners should require patentees to provide disclaimers or definitions in the specification to clarify vague claim terms; however, they should not require claim charts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requiring definitions/disclaimers helps fix term meaning contemporaneously; claim charts are discouraged. This change would increase clarity without excessive burden if done judiciously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiners should require improved written specifications (enhanced §112 enforcement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Require patentees to provide more complete written descriptions of how the invention is implemented in the preferred embodiment so readers can better understand what is and is not part of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stricter written-description enforcement would promote clarity and public notice; marginal costs are low because applicants already know their inventions. Care should be taken not to overburden inventors; focus on meaningful disclosure of implementation details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require a description of the prior art in the specification
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent applicants should be required to include a section explaining their understanding of known prior art and list preferred reference sources to reveal the applicant's view of the state of the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Benefits: reveals unwritten background, aids examiners, narrows claim construction in litigation by providing contemporaneous context, and helps identify what skills were ordinary at the filing date. Risks: could invite strategic misstatements, but duty of candor and inequitable conduct rules may limit abuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relax obviousness standard to allow examiners to consider more prior art (KSR approach)
rubrics_metrics.description: Relaxing the rigid 'teaching, suggestion, or motivation' test (per KSR) lets examiners consider predictable uses, market pressures, and 'obvious to try' considerations so more prior art can be invoked to reject obvious claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expanding obviousness review can serve the same public-notice/outer-limits function as BRC by preventing overly broad claims from issuing; traditional secondary considerations remain available to rebut obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiners should reject claims not supported by the specification (written-description requirement enforcement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners should more vigilantly reject claims that lack support in the specification under 35 U.S.C. § 112.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enforcing support requirements pressures applicants to specify and limits vagueness; this complements definition/description requirements and helps delineate claim scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intrinsic evidence controls claim meaning; extrinsic evidence disfavored
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims are to be construed primarily from intrinsic evidence—the claims, the specification, and the prosecution history—while extrinsic evidence (dictionaries, expert testimony) is admissible but disfavored and subordinate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts should rely on intrinsic record to avoid undermining public notice; extrinsic evidence only used when ambiguity persists despite intrinsic analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventor-as-lexicographer: specification definitions govern where explicit
rubrics_metrics.description: When a patent's specification provides specific definitions, those definitions control claim terms; the inventor may act as his own lexicographer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclaimers and definitions in the specification will be applied; however, disclaimers of meaning and of prior art are excluded from claim construction rules that rely on definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct claims to preserve validity if ambiguous
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim remains unclear after applying claim-construction tools, a court should construe the claim so as to be valid if possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This canon tends to produce more narrow constructions than BRC and serves as a tie-breaker favoring validity preservation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize and address examiner/applicant incentive problems (rational ignorance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants have incentives to keep claims vague (to allow ex post gaming); examiners have limited time and incentives focused on novelty/nonobviousness rather than claim clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy and procedural reforms should account for these incentives—e.g., require better specs, require definitions, relax obviousness, or change the interpretive rule—to realign incentives toward public notice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit weight of patentee/examiner testimony in construing claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Patentee testimony about claim meaning is given little weight, and patent examiners rarely testify; courts prefer contemporaneous public records over later witness testimony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relying on public record and contemporaneous specification/prosecution history reduces hindsight bias and shifting witness positions; policies that produce richer contemporaneous records (definitions, prior art descriptions) will improve claim construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-grant proceedings currently apply BRC (reexamination, reissue, interference)
rubrics_metrics.description: In post-grant processes—reexamination, reissue, and interference—the USPTO applies the broadest reasonable construction rule to the patent being reconsidered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any policy change abandoning BRC in prosecution should consider the role and rules of post-grant review and the consistency of interpretive standards across all USPTO proceedings.
